722.title: A seat at the king's table (2 Samuel 9)
722.hook: David looks for any of Saul's family to show kindness, and finds a lame grandson
722.howItsDone: Some Christians tell the story of Mephibosheth as a picture of grace and of keeping promises, and preachers use it to speak about welcoming people who have been left out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king in a plain ephod dancing before the ark, and your line was with all his might. What did you do with all your might? Day seven hundred twenty-two.

"Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul, that I may shew him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" That's the king's question, asked out loud in the palace. From a new king, a question about the old king's family could sound like a threat. Anyone listening might go quiet. They find a servant of Saul's house named Ziba, and he answers. There is one. A son of Jonathan. He lives in a place called Lo-debar, in another man's house. And Ziba adds one more detail, as if it might matter to the king: he is lame on his feet.
screen: `ANY LEFT OF THE HOUSE OF SAUL?`

segments.voice: His name is Mephibosheth. Earlier in the book we learn how he became lame: when he was five, news came that Saul and Jonathan had died, and his nurse snatched him up to flee, and in her hurry he fell. Now he's grown, with a young son of his own, the grandson of the fallen king, living away from the court in another man's house. And he's summoned to the palace. He falls on his face before David. And David's first words are: "Fear not." Then the promise, in the King James Bible: "I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually." Notice the word kindness. In Hebrew it's chesed: loyal love, the kind of faithfulness that keeps a promise. David and Jonathan had sworn to each other that their love would reach their children. Jonathan is gone. David keeps it anyway. Mephibosheth can hardly take it in. "What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?" That's how small he feels. And the chapter's last line puts the two facts side by side, with no comment: he "did eat continually at the king's table; and was lame on both his feet." Both are true. He is still lame. He still eats at the king's table. The kindness doesn't erase his story; it gives it a place. Some Christians hear their own story here: brought in from far away, given a seat they didn't earn, for someone else's sake. For them, it's a picture of grace. Others simply hear a king keeping a promise to a dead friend.
screen: `SUCH A DEAD DOG AS I AM.`

segments.voice: For this practice, plan a kindness toward an enemy's family. Let your breathing slow first. Bring to mind someone you've been at odds with, a rival, an ex, a difficult neighbor, a coworker who made life hard. Now look past them, to the people around them: a child, a parent, a partner, a friend who had nothing to do with your quarrel. What would kindness to one of them look like? A greeting. A small help. Including them instead of avoiding them. Choose one. If you pray, you can hold that person before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Mephibosheth. Jonathan's lame son, Saul's grandson, brought in by David and given a seat at the king's table as a promise of loyal love.
Your line: always at my table. Today, make room for one person you'd usually leave out, at a table, in a chat, in a plan. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

723.title: David's great wrong (2 Samuel 11)
723.hook: a king on a rooftop takes Bathsheba and arranges her husband's death
723.howItsDone: Some Christians read 2 Samuel 11 as a sobering story about the abuse of power and the way one wrong leads to the next, and read it alongside Nathan's rebuke and Psalm 51.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mephibosheth, and your line was always at my table. Whom did you make room for? Today the same king does something very different. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

The army is out in the field. The king is at home. The chapter opens "at the time when kings go forth to battle," and then adds a quiet line: "But David tarried still at Jerusalem." One evening he gets up from his bed and walks on the palace roof, and from up there he sees a woman bathing. He asks who she is. The answer comes back with her name and, pointedly, her husband's: Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. Uriah is one of his soldiers, away at the war. The king knows exactly who she is. And he sends for her anyway.

The verbs are short and they belong to the king. In the King James Bible: "David sent messengers, and took her." Sent, took. A king's messengers at the door; some readers point out that Bathsheba had little room to say no, and the text gives her no words at all until a message she sends back: "I am with child." Then the cover-up begins. David calls Uriah home from the war, makes small talk, and sends him off to his house, hoping he'll sleep with his wife and the child will seem to be his. Uriah doesn't go home. He sleeps at the palace door with the servants. And when David asks why, the soldier answers with a loyalty that shames the king: "The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife?" David gets him drunk the next night. He still doesn't go home. So David writes a letter to his general, and has Uriah carry it himself. It says: "Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die." It's done. Other soldiers die with him. When the news comes, David sends back a smooth message: don't let this trouble you; the sword devours one as well as another. Then he marries Bathsheba. For a moment it looks like he got away with it. The chapter's last line says otherwise: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." This is the same man who spared Saul in the cave. The text doesn't explain the change. Some readers point to how much power he now had, and how few people could tell him no.

Here's the practice: remember those harmed by the powerful. Settle, and breathe. Think of Bathsheba, who speaks only once in this chapter. Think of Uriah, carrying his own death warrant without knowing it. Then let your mind move to people today who have been used or silenced by someone with power over them: at work, at home, in a church, in a country. You don't need names. If you know one, hold it gently. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or in silence. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Uriah. The loyal soldier whose wife David took, and whom David then arranged to have killed in battle.
Your line: power can rot. Today, notice one place where you have power over someone, however small, and use it gently. Day seven hundred twenty-three.

724.title: You are the man (2 Samuel 12:1–13)
724.hook: Nathan tells a story about a poor man's lamb, and David convicts himself
724.carry: I have sinned against the Lord
724.howItsDone: Some Christians read Nathan's rebuke together with Psalm 51, whose heading links it to this moment, and some pray Psalm 51 as a prayer of confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uriah, and your line was power can rot. Where did you have power over someone, and how did you use it? Day seven hundred twenty-four.

Uriah is dead. Bathsheba lives in David's house. A son is born. The text records no one saying a word to the king. Then the prophet Nathan comes, sent by God. He doesn't accuse anyone. He asks the king for a ruling on a case. There were two men in one city, he says, one rich and one poor. The rich man had flocks and herds, a great many. The poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb. And David, who was a shepherd before he was a king, leans in to listen.
screen: `A SON IS BORN. NO ONE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Listen to how Nathan describes that lamb, in the King James Bible: it "grew up together with him, and with his children; it did eat of his own meat, and drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was unto him as a daughter." A pet. Family. Then a traveler comes to visit the rich man, and the rich man doesn't want to take from his own flock, so he takes the poor man's lamb, and serves it for dinner. David explodes. "As the LORD liveth, the man that hath done this thing shall surely die." He orders the lamb repaid fourfold, because the man did this thing and had no pity. He has pronounced the sentence. And then Nathan says it, in the old English: "Thou art the man." The story was a mirror, and David walked right up to it. Nathan goes on in God's name: I anointed you, I gave you everything, and if that had been too little I would have given you more. Why did you despise the commandment? You killed Uriah with the sword of the Ammonites, and took his wife. The man with all the flocks took the one lamb. A king could have had him thrown out. David doesn't. He says: "I have sinned against the LORD." No excuse. No list of reasons. Nathan answers at once: "The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die." Forgiven, though the chapter goes on to say there will still be consequences. The heading of Psalm fifty-one ties that psalm to this very moment, when Nathan came to David. Some Christians pray that psalm as a prayer of repentance.

Now, the practice: let one hard truth in. Get still, and breathe. Think of the last time someone told you something true about yourself that you didn't want to hear. A friend, a partner, a child, a boss, a stranger. Maybe you pushed it away. Maybe you argued. Go back to it now, slowly. Ask one question only: was any of it true? If some of it was, don't defend yourself in your head. Just let it stand there, like Nathan in the doorway. If you pray, you can bring it before God in silence. The bell holds the time.
Nathan. The prophet who told David a story about a rich man and a poor man's lamb, until the king realized he was the guilty judge.
Your line: I have sinned against the Lord. Today, if someone tells you a hard truth, say thank you before you say anything else. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

725.title: Absalom, my son (2 Samuel 18:33)
725.hook: David's rebel son dies and the king weeps: would I had died for you
725.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to David's lament for Absalom when speaking of a parent's grief, and some hear in it a picture of God's love for those who have turned away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan and the poor man's lamb, and your line was I have sinned against the Lord. What hard truth did you let in? Day seven hundred twenty-five.

Two runners are coming across the plain. The king is sitting between the two gates of the city, waiting, and a watchman on the roof of the gate calls down what he sees. The battle is over. It was a battle against David's own son. Absalom, the handsome one, praised in all Israel for his looks, had stolen the people's hearts, declared himself king, and driven his father out of Jerusalem. Now the armies have met in a forest. The first runner arrives: good news, the king's enemies are defeated. David asks only one question. Not who won. Not how many fell. Is the young man Absalom safe?

Before the battle, David gave his generals one order, in front of the whole army: "Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom." It wasn't obeyed. Absalom rode his mule under the thick branches of a great oak, his head caught fast, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth. The general Joab, who had heard the king's order, thrust three darts into him as he hung there, and Joab's armor-bearers finished it. The second runner arrives, and David asks again: is the young man safe? The runner says it gently: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. And David understands. Here is the verse, in the King James Bible: "And the king was much moved, and went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept: and as he went, thus he said, O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!" Read it aloud and it barely holds together. It isn't a speech. It's a man climbing to a room over a gate, saying the same few words over and over. This son had tried to take his throne. Some readers hear in it, too, the shadow of Nathan's words: trouble rising from David's own house. None of that stops the grief. The king who won the battle says he would rather have died himself. The text counts the cost as well: the soldiers come back into the city quietly that day, like people ashamed, because their victory had turned into mourning. Christians have heard this verse in more than one way. One reading is simple: a parent's love that outlasts betrayal, that would trade places with the child who wronged him. Some Christians hear in it an echo of their teaching about Jesus: that God did what David could only wish, and died for those who had turned away.
screen: `WOULD GOD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a grieving parent in mind. Settle, and breathe. Some of us know a mother or father who has lost a child, through death, or estrangement, or a road the child chose. Some of us are that parent. If someone comes to mind, let them come, gently. Don't try to say anything wise about it. David's words barely hold together, and that's allowed. Just sit with them in the room over the gate for a minute. If you pray, you can pray for them in silence, or in your own words. If you don't, simply hold them with care. The bell holds the time.
Absalom. David's son, who rebelled against him and died in the forest, and whom the king mourned: would God I had died for thee.
Your line: my son, my son. Today, reach out to one parent you know who is carrying a loss, with a message, a call, or just their name in your thoughts. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

726.title: Solomon's request (1 Kings 3:5–14)
726.hook: asked what he wants, a young king asks for an understanding heart
726.howItsDone: Some Christians pray for wisdom with Solomon's request in mind, and some point to James 1:5, which invites anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Absalom, and your line was my son, my son. Whom did you hold in mind? David's story is ending, and his son Solomon now sits on the throne. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

"Ask what I shall give thee." Those are the words. No conditions, no small print. The new king Solomon has gone to Gibeon to offer sacrifices, and that night, in a dream, God appears to him and says them. Ask. Whatever you want. It's the old game of one wish, except here God is the one asking, and the person being asked is young, newly crowned, with his father David just gone and a whole kingdom watching to see what kind of king he'll be. What would anyone ask for? Money that never runs out. A long life. Enemies out of the way. Solomon asks for none of them.

He starts by being honest about himself. In the King James Bible: "I am but a little child: I know not how to go out or come in." A king, admitting he doesn't know how to do the job. Then the request: "Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad." In Hebrew, the phrase for an understanding heart is lev shomea: literally, a hearing heart, a listening heart. Some readers point out that in the Bible's way of speaking, the heart is where you think and decide, not only where you feel. So Solomon is asking for a mind that listens: to people, to both sides of a case, to God. And notice who it's for. Not for himself. To judge thy people. He wants to be good at serving them. The text says the speech pleased the Lord, and God names everything Solomon didn't ask for: "thou hast not asked for thyself long life; neither hast asked riches for thyself, nor hast asked the life of thine enemies." And here's the turn: God gives him the wise and understanding heart, and then adds the things he didn't ask for, riches and honor, and long life if he walks in God's ways. Some Christians connect this with a line from the Gospels: seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest will be added. The letter of James puts it plainly too: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God." The story doesn't promise that Solomon always used his gift well; later chapters are honest about that. But on this night, with anything in the world on offer, he asked for a listening heart.

The practice today: ask for wisdom, not stuff. Take a slow breath first. Think of one situation in your life right now where you don't know what to do: a decision, a conflict, a person you can't read. Notice what you'd normally wish for: that it would just go away, or go your way. Set that wish down. Instead, ask for a listening heart for this one situation. If you pray, you can ask God for it in your own words, or borrow Solomon's: an understanding heart. If you don't pray, simply hold the situation and listen, without deciding anything yet. The bell holds the time.
Solomon's request. Offered anything at all, the young king asked for an understanding heart, to judge his people well.
Your line: an understanding heart. Today, before you decide one thing, hear out the side you'd rather not hear. Day seven hundred twenty-six.

727.title: Two mothers (1 Kings 3:16–28)
727.hook: a sword, a baby, and the real mother gives him up to save him
727.howItsDone: Some Christians read the judgment of Solomon as the wisdom he asked for in 1 Kings 3 put into practice, and some preachers dwell on the true mother as a picture of self-giving love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon's request: offered anything, a young king asked to judge well. Your line was an understanding heart. Where did you listen before you answered? Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

Two women stand before the king, and only one of them is telling the truth. They share a house. Each has given birth, a few days apart. One night one of the babies died, and now both women claim the living one. The text is careful to say there was no stranger in the house, only the two of them. So there are no witnesses. One says: she swapped them while I slept. The other says: no, the living one is mine, the dead one is yours. Back and forth, in front of the throne. This is the young king who has just asked for an understanding heart, and here is a case with no way in. No evidence. Nothing to check. Just two voices and one child. Today, two mothers.

The king says one short line: "Bring me a sword." Then the order: divide the living child in two, half to one woman and half to the other. It sounds monstrous, and it's meant to. Solomon isn't looking for the answer in the facts, because there aren't any. He builds a moment where the answer has to show itself. And it does. In the King James Bible, the real mother speaks "for her bowels yearned upon her son." That's older English for something deep in the body: everything inside her turned toward him. She says, "O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it." Give him to her. She surrenders the case. She loses on purpose, to keep him breathing. The other woman says, "Let it be neither mine nor thine, but divide it." Listen to what she wants: not the child, but for nobody to have him. Then the king answers by repeating the first mother's own words back, and adding one line: "Give her the living child, and in no wise slay it: she is the mother thereof." The proof that she's his mother is that she was willing to stop being called his mother. Some readers hear the story mainly as a portrait of Solomon, and the chapter ends that way: all Israel heard, and saw "that the wisdom of God was in him, to do judgment." Other readers notice that the real wisdom in the room might belong to the woman whose name we never learn, who knew that winning and loving had come apart, and chose the child. Either way, it's yesterday's request put to work: a heart that can hear the difference between someone who wants to be right and someone who wants the child to live.

Here's the practice: find one fight you could stop trying to win. Settle, and breathe. Let one ongoing argument come to mind: with a partner, a sibling, a coworker, a kid. Ask what it would cost to stop needing to win it. Not to agree. Not to pretend. Just to set the winning down, for the sake of the person, or the thing the two of you share. Picture the two of you a year from now, and ask which matters more then: the point, or the person. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, keep their face in mind and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Two mothers. One wanted to win, one wanted the child alive, and the king told them apart by what each was willing to give up.
Your line: the real mother. Today, in one small disagreement, let the other person have it, for the sake of what's between you. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.

728.title: The temple dedicated (1 Kings 8:22–30)
728.hook: heaven can't contain you, how much less this house
728.howItsDone: Some churches hold a service of dedication when a new building opens, and Solomon's prayer in 1 Kings 8, with its admission that heaven cannot contain God, may be read there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two mothers and a sword. Your line was the real mother. Did you let someone else have something small, for the sake of what's between you? Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

The house is finished. Cedar, stone, gold. The ark has been carried into the inner room, and a cloud has filled the house, so that, the text says, the priests could not stand to minister. Now Solomon stands before the altar, in front of the whole congregation of Israel, and spreads his hands toward heaven. It's his moment. The work is done, and a crowd is waiting. A builder's speech would be easy here: look what we made. What comes out of his mouth instead is a question that almost undoes the building. Today, the temple dedicated.

Here's the question, in the King James Bible: "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?" He says it on opening day. Heaven can't hold you, and neither can heaven's heaven, so this house certainly can't. Then what is the house for? Solomon answers in the next breath. He doesn't ask God to move in. He asks God to look: "That thine eyes may be open toward this house night and day." And to listen. When your people pray toward this place, he says, "hear thou in heaven thy dwelling place: and when thou hearest, forgive." Notice where the hearing happens. In heaven. The house is not a box for God. It's a direction, a place to turn your face. And as the prayer goes on, Solomon pictures people praying toward it from far away: a stranger who comes from a distant country, his own people carried off into a foreign land, turning toward the city and the house. Later, the book of Daniel shows a man in exile doing just that, praying with his windows open toward Jerusalem. Christians carry this prayer in more than one way. Some hear an echo in John's Gospel: "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Others point to Paul, who tells a church, "ye are the temple of God." And some simply carry Solomon's question into the churches they build: a house that can't hold God, opened anyway as a place to turn and pray.

Here's the practice: face a place. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place that's holy to you, or simply dear: a church, a grave, a grandmother's kitchen, a hill you used to climb. If you know which way it lies, turn toward it. If you don't, face a window. Solomon didn't ask God to live in his place, only to keep eyes open toward it. If you pray, you can pray toward that place now, in silence or in your own words. If you don't, let it be the direction of your attention for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Solomon. The king who, on the day his temple opened, admitted heaven itself can't contain God, and asked only for open eyes and a listening ear toward it.

Your line: heaven cannot contain you. This week ran from Mephibosheth, through Uriah and a father's grief, to a wise request, two mothers and a finished house. Today, let one ordinary place become a direction you pause toward. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

fork.setup: you're Solomon. the house is finished, the whole congregation is watching, and you spread your hands toward heaven. what do you say about the house?
options: here, at last, God will live among us.
will God indeed dwell on the earth? this house can't contain you.
look at the cedar and gold we gave.
fork.reveal: on opening day he admits the house can't hold God, and asks instead that God's eyes be open toward it, and that God hear, and forgive.

original.note: Hebrew: house, the plain word Solomon uses for the temple: how much less this house (1 Kings 8:27).

trapdoor: what you thought: a king cutting the ribbon on a building.
what it means: a builder's prayer that admits the building can't hold God, and asks for open eyes and forgiveness instead.
what a scholar hears: God hears 'in heaven thy dwelling place' (8:30); the house is where people turn to pray, even strangers and exiles far away (8:41–48).
